summary: This informational document covers problems with dynamic DNS when address sharing is used during IPv6 transition, such as with DS-Lite and NAT64. It documents issues and possible solutions, using the Port Control Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: When many customers share one public Internet address, a home server does not get the usual port, so the name it publishes in the phone book also has to include the address and port it is using right now. RFC 7393 explains how the Port Control Protocol can tell a dynamic DNS client these details, and how a DNS provider can help visitors reach the server.

questions: dns update behind shared ipv4 address
how does ddns work with ds-lite
why is address-sharing a problem for ddns
subtitle: Keeping a home server reachable when an address-sharing network gives it a non-standard port instead of the usual one.

tldr.problem: In address-sharing networks such as DS-Lite and NAT64, a customer device no longer gets the well-known port for its server, and dynamic DNS can only publish a domain name if it also learns the assigned external address and port and notices when either changes.
tldr.mechanism: The memo shows how the Port Control Protocol (PCP) can install a port mapping and report the external IP address and port, letting a DDNS client refresh DNS records; it also sketches how a DDNS server can redirect or list services so users reach the right coordinates.
tldr.outcome: The document specifies no protocol extension: it is operational guidance for DDNS providers, reusing PCP and standard DNS updates as they are.

facts.value: MAP request installs a mapping and reports the external IP address and port

facts.value: HTTP 301 to the external address and port

facts.value: None; no PCP or DNS update extension

today: RFC 7393 is an Informational RFC from November 2014. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It specifies no protocol extension and no changes to PCP or DNS updates; it remains operational guidance for combining PCP with dynamic DNS in address-sharing deployments.

sections.title: The Address-Sharing Problem for Dynamic DNS
sections.content:
Dynamic DNS (DDNS) keeps a domain name pointed at a device's current IP address. It is widely used so that people can host a server, such as a webcam or an HTTP or FTP server, on an ordinary connection. A DDNS client, usually running on the user's router or computer, notices when the assigned IP address changes and sends an update to a DDNS server. The traffic between client and server is not standardized and varies between providers, though some standard web-based update methods have emerged.

Address sharing breaks that model. In contexts such as Dual-Stack Lite (DS-Lite) and NAT64, well-known ports such as port 80 are not available to every user. A customer device therefore cannot be reached on the default port, and the DDNS client has to register not just the IP address but also the external port that its service listens on, then report any change to either. Making incoming connections work also requires configuring a port mapping on the Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN), so that traffic from the Internet reaches the right server behind it.

The document lists three challenges: the DDNS service must be able to announce and store an alternate service port; the address-sharing device must be given explicit mappings so incoming connections get through; and the DDNS client must detect changes to the external IP address or port and refresh the DNS records. The last problem is worse under DS-Lite, because no public IPv4 address is assigned to the Customer Premises Equipment at all.
sections.plainLanguage: A dynamic DNS service keeps a name pointing at whatever address a device has right now. When many customers share one public address, the device also gets an unusual port, and the service must publish that port and follow it as it changes, or visitors cannot reach the device.

sections.title: The Solution Space
sections.content:
The RFC describes candidate solutions with a focus on DS-Lite, and says they apply to other address-sharing schemes too. Everything rests on the Port Control Protocol (PCP): it is used to install the mapping in the CGN so that incoming packets are delivered to the right server, and it lets a client ask what external IP address and port it has.

Before a visitor can reach the service, the assigned port has to be conveyed somehow. The document names two ways to associate a port number with a service: use service URIs, such as FTP, SIP or HTTP, that carry the port in their syntax (for example mydomain.example:15687), or use SRV records, which most browsers do not support. In either case the DDNS client and the DDNS server are updated so the alternate port is signalled and stored, and requesting remote hosts are told which IP address and port to use.

The memo is careful about its scope. DDNS can be seen as one implementation of the rendezvous function of PCP, which tells remote hosts the address, protocol and port to use, but PCP itself does not provide that function. This document specifies no protocol extension and requires no changes to PCP or to standard DNS dynamic updates; it is an operational document that shows how existing tools can be reused.
sections.plainLanguage: Two pieces must come together: a mapping in the shared device that lets traffic in, and a way to tell the world which address and port to use. The Port Control Protocol handles the mapping and reports the details, and the document reuses existing tools rather than inventing new ones.

sections.title: Detecting Address and Port Changes
sections.content:
Because the external coordinates can change, the DDNS client has to keep checking them. The RFC gives two periodic approaches, both run by a client on the Customer Premises Equipment (CPE) or on the host running the service.

In the first, the client issues PCP MAP requests with short lifetimes, for example 30 seconds, on a long interval such as every 60 minutes, to learn its external IP address and to set up the mapping. If the external IP address changes, the client updates the DNS records accordingly. In the second, the client reads the local mapping table that the PCP client maintains, checking on a schedule such as every 5, 30 or 60 minutes; if no mapping exists, it sends a PCP MAP request to learn the external address and set up forwarding, and again pushes a DNS update when the address changes.

The remainder of the flow is a normal message exchange: the client sends a PCP MAP request, the CGN or PCP server answers with the external address and port, and the client tells the DDNS server about any change so it can pass the update on to the DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: The client cannot assume its address and port stay the same, so it asks the shared device on a schedule. When the answer differs from last time, the client tells the DNS provider so the name keeps pointing at the right place.

sections.title: Deployment for Web and Non-Web Services
sections.content:
The RFC sets out a reference topology in which an end user reaches a DDNS server, which sits in front of the address-sharing device, the customer's PCP and DDNS clients, and the servers themselves. The address-sharing device, called the AFTR, keeps the mappings between the internal address and port and the external address and port; the DDNS server keeps the mapping between a registered domain name and the registered external IP address and port.

For a web service, the DDNS server cannot assume the web server sits on port 80. When a visitor's browser sends an HTTP GET after resolving the name, the DDNS server replies with an HTTP 301 redirect pointing at the actual external address and port, and the request then reaches the AFTR and is forwarded to the right host behind it. For example, a request can be redirected to 192.0.2.1:8001, which the AFTR forwards to the web server at 192.0.2.1:8000 internally.

For non-web services, an HTTP redirect is not enough, so the RFC describes a web portal. The DDNS client registers the public IP address and port obtained through PCP, the user's fully qualified domain name, and other details. The DDNS server runs a portal for each registered name and lists the available services with their current links, such as http://192.0.2.1:2000 or rtsp://192.0.2.1:8080/test.sdp. A visitor who looks up the name reaches the portal and can follow a link to the service. Applications that are not HTTP based can be delivered the same way, though invoking them is outside the document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: For websites, the DNS provider sends the visitor on to the real address and port. For other services, it keeps a page for each customer that lists what is available and where, so a visitor can click through to the service directly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document introduces no new protocol and no protocol extensions, so the security considerations of PCP and DS-Lite apply as they are. The crux is that the link between the DDNS client and the DDNS server is proprietary in most cases, and providers may need to extend it.

Because the DDNS server is what publishes names and addresses, it is the natural target. Operators should enforce security policies that stop illegitimate users from changing records that belong to someone else, or from installing fake records that would attract traffic to an attacker's device. Protection against Denial of Service should also be enabled. The RFC notes that these concerns are not specific to address sharing and apply to DDNS services in general.
sections.plainLanguage: The address-sharing network adds no new protocol, so the usual protections for PCP and DS-Lite still apply. The DNS provider must make sure only the real owner can change a name's records, and it must be able to withstand attacks that try to flood it.
